title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 32
paragraphs: So Solon assigned the second place in happiness to these men, and Croesus, provoked to anger, said: “Athenian guest, have you then cast aside our prosperity as worth nothing, so that you prefer even private citizens to us?” And Solon said: “Croesus, you are questioning about human fortunes a man who knows well that the deity is altogether envious and given to disturbing our lot. For in the course of a long life a man is bound to see many things he would not wish to see, and to suffer many things he would not wish to suffer. I set the limit of a man’s life at seventy years. These seventy years give twenty-five thousand two hundred days, without counting any intercalary month. And if every second year is lengthened by a month so that the seasons may come round at their due time, the intercalated months over the seventy years will number thirty-five, and the days in those months will be one thousand and fifty. So of all these days in the seventy years—twenty-six thousand two hundred and fifty in total—no single day produces anything at all like what another brings with it. Thus, Croesus, man is altogether a creature of chance. As for you, I see that you are both great in wealth and king over many men; but what you asked me I cannot yet call you, until I learn that you have brought your life to a fair ending. For the very rich man is no happier than the man who has only his daily subsistence, unless good fortune also attends him so that he ends his life well while still in possession of all fair things. For many very wealthy men are not happy, while many who have only a moderate living are fortunate. In truth the rich man who is not happy has only two advantages over the poor man who is fortunate, whereas the poor fortunate man has many advantages over him. The rich man is better able to fulfill his desires, and to endure a great calamity if it falls upon him; but the other surpasses him in these ways: he is not indeed able to endure calamity or fulfill desire as well as the rich man, yet his good fortune keeps such things away from him, while he is sound of limb, free from disease, untouched by suffering, father of fair children, and himself of comely form. And if in addition he ends his life well, he is worthy to be called that which you are seeking—a happy man. But before he comes to his end, it is well to hold back and not yet call him happy, but only fortunate. Now to possess all these things together is impossible for any mere mortal, just as no single land suffices to supply everything for itself, but has one thing and lacks another, and the land that has the greatest number is the best. So too in the case of a man: no single person is complete in himself; he has one thing and lacks another. But whoever continues to the end in possession of the greatest number of these things and then comes to a gracious ending of his life—this man, O king, I judge worthy to receive this name. In every matter we must examine the end and how it will turn out at last, for to many men God has shown a glimpse of happiness and then uprooted and overturned them.”
